name: Kalimpong and Neora
tagline: Old trade town, quiet villages, red panda forest
meta_description: Plan Kalimpong, Lava, Lolegaon, Rishyap, Pedong and Neora Valley for less: shared jeeps, homestays, real costs, honest seasons and the stories behind the hills.
summary: Kalimpong is the quieter, cheaper neighbour of Darjeeling: a market town on a ridge above the Teesta, with village homestays, pine forest at Lava and Lolegaon, and the Neora Valley, home of the red panda. Plan 3 to 6 nights from Siliguri, October to May, with shared jeeps and homestays to keep costs low.
intro: Kalimpong sits on a ridge at about 1,250 m between two hills, Deolo and Durpin, with the Teesta river far below. It is a working town before it is a tourist town: schools, nurseries, a twice-weekly haat, monasteries and Scottish mission churches. Most visitors give it a day on the way to somewhere else. We think it deserves two nights, and the villages around it deserve more.

The district only became its own district on 14 February 2017, carved out of Darjeeling. Before that it was a subdivision, and before 1865 it was not British at all but part of Bhutan. That layered past shows everywhere: a Bhutanese-era monastery near the market, Tibetan traders' families who still run shops, Lepcha villages that were here before any of them, and Gorkha farmers who terraced the slopes.

East of the town the road climbs through Algarah to Lava at about 2,200 m, the gateway to Neora Valley National Park. From Lava, short drives reach Rishyap, Kolakham and Lolegaon, each a cluster of homestays with Kanchenjunga on a clear morning. North-east, Pedong and Sillery Gaon sit on the old trade route that ran over Jelep La into Tibet, now the start of the Silk Route drive to Zuluk.

This is good country for a careful budget. A shared jeep from Siliguri costs a few hundred rupees, homestay rooms with meals are often cheaper than a town hotel, and many of the best things are free: sunrise at Tiffin Dara, the walk round Durpin, the Wednesday and Saturday haat. Spend where it matters, on a good driver for the village roads and a guide in the national park.

story.title: How a Bhutanese hill became a wool market
paras: Until 1865 the ridge where Kalimpong now stands belonged to Bhutan. After the Duar War of 1864–65, Bhutan signed the Treaty of Sinchula on 11 November 1865 and ceded the hill tract east of the Teesta, together with the plains Duars, to British India in return for an annual subsidy. The tract was attached to Darjeeling district, and a small village of a few households started to grow.

Its fortune came from the north. The easiest pass between Sikkim and Tibet's Chumbi Valley was Jelep La, at about 4,270 m, and Kalimpong was the nearest market town on the Indian side. Mule caravans brought Tibetan wool, furs and yak tails down the trail through Pedong and Algarah, and went back with cloth, tea, metal goods and sugar. Wool was baled in Kalimpong godowns and sent on to the plains and Calcutta.

Missionaries, traders and families followed. Rev. William Macfarlane of the Church of Scotland opened the first schools in the early 1870s, and Rev. John Anderson Graham founded the cottage homes that became Dr. Graham's Homes in 1900. The trade ended when Jelep La was closed after the 1962 India–China war. The town kept its schools, its nurseries and the Tibetan, Bhutanese and Marwari families who had settled for the trade, and that mix is what you walk through today.
story.source: Duar War and Treaty of Sinchula (1865); Jelep La; Kalimpong and Dr. Graham's Homes articles on Wikipedia; Bengal District Gazetteer

did_you_know: Kalimpong was part of Bhutan until the Treaty of Sinchula of 11 November 1865, which ended the Duar War.
Kalimpong became a separate district of West Bengal on 14 February 2017, carved out of Darjeeling district.
The Dalai Lama consecrated the Zang Dhok Palri Phodang monastery on Durpin Hill in 1976, and it keeps 108 volumes of the Kangyur brought from Tibet.
Jelep La, the old trade pass between Kalimpong and Tibet's Chumbi Valley, was closed after the 1962 India–China war and has not reopened to trade.
Neora Valley National Park, set up in 1986, covers about 88 sq km and is one of the few protected habitats of the red panda in West Bengal.
facts: Nepali, Hindi, Bengali, English; Lepcha and Tibetan spoken in some homes
None for Indians; Neora Valley entry permit from the forest office at Lava
About 250 m (Teesta Bazaar) to 3,200 m (Rachela Danda)

highlights.title: Durpin and Deolo ridges
highlights.text: Kalimpong hangs between two hills. Walk or drive up Durpin for the Zang Dhok Palri monastery and the Teesta valley, and up Deolo, the highest point at 1,704 m, for the town's reservoirs, a park and a wide view to the snows of West Sikkim.

highlights.title: Lava and the Neora forest
highlights.text: At about 2,200 m, Lava is a small bazaar town with a large Kagyu monastery and the forest office that issues Neora Valley permits. From here a jeep track runs to Zero Point inside the park, where fir, oak and rhododendron forest shelters the red panda.

highlights.title: Village homestays
highlights.text: Lolegaon, Rishyap, Kolakham, Sillery Gaon, Icchey Gaon and Ramdhura each have a handful of family homestays where rooms come with home-cooked meals. You trade town comforts for silence, birdsong and a good chance of a clear Kanchenjunga at dawn.

highlights.title: The old Tibet road
highlights.text: Pedong and Algarah sat on the mule route to Jelep La. Damsang Fort, linked in Lepcha tradition to Gaeboo Achyok, a 1706 Bhutanese-era monastery and a cross raised in 1882 by a French priest bound for Tibet all lie within a short drive of each other.

highlights.title: Nurseries and orchids
highlights.text: Kalimpong grows and exports flowers, bulbs and cacti. About 300 orchid species occur around the town, and family nurseries, some open to visitors, sell gladioli, amaryllis and cactus. Spring, March to May, is when most things are in flower.

highlights.title: Food with a history
highlights.text: Kalimpong cheese and the milk lollipops sold in every shop go back to a Swiss Jesuit dairy started in the 1950s. Add Tibetan thukpa and shaphaley, Nepali sel roti and gundruk, and hard yak-milk churpi from the haat, all at modest prices.

getting_there: Fly to Bagdogra (IXB) or take a train to New Jalpaiguri (NJP), both near Siliguri. Kalimpong is about 70–80 km away, normally 2.5–3.5 hours by road along the Teesta through Sevoke and Teesta Bazaar on NH10. Shared jeeps leave Siliguri for Kalimpong through the day, and NBSTC buses run from the Siliguri bus terminus. A reserved car from the airport or station suits families and late arrivals. Since the October 2023 Teesta flood, NH10 has had repeated closures; drivers then use the longer route through Malbazar, Gorubathan and Lava, or via Darjeeling and Peshok. Pakyong airport in Sikkim is about 56 km away, but flights there have been irregular. Check current status before you travel.
permits: Indian citizens need no permit for Kalimpong, Lava, Lolegaon, Rishyap, Pedong or the villages. Foreign nationals also need no special permit for Kalimpong district. Neora Valley National Park needs a day-entry permit from the forest range office at Lava, with a vehicle fee and a guide; the park is closed in the monsoon, usually from 16 June to 15 September. The Silk Route beyond Pedong enters East Sikkim, where Zuluk and the Old Silk Route need a permit arranged through a registered Sikkim operator, and foreigners are generally not allowed. Check current status before you travel.

budget.summary: Kalimpong already costs less than Darjeeling or Gangtok, and you can trim further without a worse trip. Use shared jeeps for the long transfer from Siliguri, book one reserved car only for the village days when there is no public transport, sleep in homestays where dinner and breakfast are included, and travel in March, early April, October or November on weekdays. Avoid the Puja and Christmas weeks, when Kolkata families fill every room.
costs: Reserved car NJP or IXB → Kalimpong
Neora Valley entry, vehicle and guide
About ₹1,500–2,500 for a small group, indicative, 2026
Thali or thukpa in a local eatery
tips: Take a shared jeep from Siliguri to Kalimpong and a reserved car only from Kalimpong onwards, which can save ₹2,000 or more per car.
Choose homestays with dinner and breakfast included; village eateries are few and a meal plan is cheaper than ordering à la carte.
Do the Kalimpong town sights as a half-day on foot and by shared taxi instead of the standard full-day 'point' tour.
Travel Monday to Thursday; weekend rates in Lava and Lolegaon rise when Siliguri and Kolkata visitors arrive.
Combine Lava, Rishyap and Kolakham from one base instead of moving every night, which cuts car costs.

months.weather: Kalimpong 6–15 °C, Lava near freezing at night, dry
months.summary: Cold and clear. Kalimpong is pleasant by day and chilly after dark, while Lava and Rishyap drop near freezing and occasionally see snow. Visibility is often excellent, so Kanchenjunga views from Rishyap, Lolegaon and Deolo are at their best. Neora Valley is open and good for winter birds. Bring proper woollens and expect homestays to have limited heating.
months.tip: Pack a thermal layer and a hot-water bottle; most village homestays have no room heaters.
months.price_note: Low season after New Year: many homestays and hotels discount weekday rooms.

months.summary: Still cold up high but the days lengthen. Losar falls in February or March in most years, so Kalimpong's monasteries and Tibetan families celebrate the new year with prayers and food. Neora Valley birding is good, with winter visitors still around. Haze starts to build late in the month on some days.
months.tip: Ask your homestay whether Losar falls during your stay; the date follows the lunar calendar.
months.price_note: Quiet month: good room availability and fair rates outside long weekends.

months.summary: Spring begins. Rhododendrons start to flower in the Neora forests and around Lava and Rishyap, nurseries in Kalimpong fill with colour, and the air is mild. Mornings are often clear, though haze can soften the views by afternoon. A good month for walks between villages and for the nurseries in Kalimpong.
months.tip: Start walks early; clouds tend to build over the snows after 10 am.
months.price_note: Rates climb toward Holi weekend; weekdays remain good value.

months.summary: Peak spring. Rhododendron and magnolia flower higher up, orchids bloom in nurseries, and the birding in Neora Valley is excellent as breeding begins. Afternoon showers arrive late in the month. Bengali New Year in mid-April brings visitors from Kolkata, so book ahead.
months.tip: Book Lava and Lolegaon forest lodges well before the mid-April holiday weekend.
months.price_note: Busy around Poila Baisakh; expect full occupancy and firm rates that week.

months.summary: School holidays bring families from Kolkata and the plains, escaping the heat. Days are warm and green, with rain most afternoons by late May. Mountain views are less reliable, but forest walks, nurseries and the Teesta are at their liveliest. Book transport and rooms early.
months.tip: Plan sightseeing for mornings and keep afternoons free for rain.
months.price_note: Peak family season: highest rates of spring, and cars are in short supply.

months.summary: The monsoon arrives around mid-June. Neora Valley closes to visitors from 16 June, roads start to suffer landslides, and the Teesta rises. Early June can still work for a short Kalimpong stay, but we do not plan village circuits after the rains settle in. Leeches appear on forest paths.
months.tip: Keep a spare day for road closures if you must travel in June.
months.price_note: Rates fall sharply once the rains set in; good deals for flexible travellers.

months.summary: The wettest month, with rain most days and frequent landslides on NH10 and the village roads. Neora Valley is closed. The hills are deep green and empty, and Kalimpong town itself can be pleasant for a rainy, bookish stay, but this is not a month for a planned tour.
months.tip: If you travel, stay in one place and avoid long road days.
months.price_note: Lowest prices of the year; many homestays offer large discounts.

months.summary: Still the full monsoon. Landslides close roads for hours or days, and river rafting stops. Waterfalls such as Changey are at their fullest but hard to reach. Lepcha families mark Tendong Lho Rum Faat in early August. Plan only short stays with flexible dates.
months.tip: Watch the district administration's road updates before driving.
months.price_note: Off-season prices continue; very few visitors outside the long weekend of 15 August.

months.summary: Rain eases through the month and Neora Valley reopens on 16 September. Dashain often begins in late September or early October. The second half of the month can bring fresh, washed views, though showers continue. Roads may still carry monsoon damage.
months.tip: Leave the national park for the last week, after the reopening.
months.price_note: Shoulder-season rates hold until Puja bookings begin.

months.summary: Post-monsoon clarity makes October one of the best months for Kanchenjunga views. Dashain and Durga Puja bring crowds from Kolkata, so the Puja week is busy and expensive. After it, the hills are calm, green and clear, and every village homestay is open.
months.tip: Travel in the two weeks after Durga Puja for clear skies and fair prices.
months.price_note: Puja week is the most expensive of the year; rates drop a week later.

months.summary: Dry, cool and usually clear, November is our favourite month here. Tihar lights up houses in late October or November. Birding in Neora improves as altitudinal migrants come down. Nights at Lava and Rishyap are cold, so pack layers.
months.tip: Plan dawn at Tiffin Dara or Jhandi Dara; November mornings are the clearest.
months.price_note: Good value after Tihar, until the Christmas rush.

months.summary: Cold, clear and festive. Kalimpong's mission churches, MacFarlane among them, hold Christmas services and carols, and the last week of December fills with Kolkata holidaymakers. Earlier in the month is quiet and very clear. Lepchas gather at Damsang on 20 December to remember Gaeboo Achyok.
months.tip: Book Christmas and New Year rooms by October.
months.price_note: Quiet and cheap early in the month, then peak rates from 22 December to New Year.

faqs.q: Is Kalimpong worth visiting or is Darjeeling better
faqs.a: Kalimpong is worth at least two nights, and it suits travellers who want a calmer, cheaper base. Darjeeling has the toy train and famous tea estates; Kalimpong has monasteries, nurseries, mission history, and quick access to village homestays at Lava, Lolegaon and Rishyap. Many of our guests do both: two or three nights in Darjeeling, then two in Kalimpong, about 50 km and 2.5 hours apart by road.

faqs.q: How many days are enough for Kalimpong and Lava
faqs.a: Plan four nights for a relaxed trip: two in Kalimpong for the town, Durpin, Deolo and the nurseries, and two in Lava for Neora Valley, Rishyap and Changey Falls. With three nights, do one in Kalimpong and two in Lava. Add a night in Lolegaon or Sillery Gaon if you want a village stay. Allow a half-day for the drive from Siliguri.

faqs.q: How much is a shared jeep from Siliguri to Kalimpong
faqs.a: Expect ₹200–300 a seat, indicative for 2026. Shared jeeps and smaller cars leave from the stands near Siliguri's bus terminus and Panitanki More when full, from early morning until mid-afternoon. The ride takes 2.5 to 3.5 hours depending on the road. A reserved car for the same trip costs about ₹3,000–4,500. Fares change with fuel prices and road diversions, so check before you go.

faqs.q: When is the best time to visit Kalimpong
faqs.a: October to early December and March to April are best. Post-monsoon October and November give the clearest Kanchenjunga views, while March and April bring rhododendrons, orchids and the best birding in Neora Valley. Winter is clear but cold up at Lava. Avoid mid-June to mid-September, when heavy rain causes landslides and Neora Valley is closed.

NH10 along the Teesta is the main road, but since the October 2023 flood it has closed often, especially in the monsoon, because of washouts and landslides. When it closes, cars use the route through Malbazar, Gorubathan and Lava, or through Darjeeling and Peshok, which add one to three hours. Check current status before you travel and keep your first day flexible.

faqs.q: Do I need a permit for Kalimpong or Lava
faqs.a: No. Indian and foreign visitors need no permit for Kalimpong, Lava, Lolegaon, Rishyap, Pedong or the villages. You do need a day-entry permit from the forest range office at Lava to enter Neora Valley National Park, and Sikkim permits if you continue on the Silk Route to Zuluk. Rules can change, so check current status before you travel.

faqs.q: Can I see a red panda in Neora Valley
faqs.a: It is possible but rare. Neora Valley is one of the red panda's protected habitats in West Bengal, but the animals are shy, live high in the canopy, and most visitors never see one. Your best chance is a quiet early-morning walk with a forest guide beyond Zero Point between November and April. Go for the forest and birds, and treat a panda as a bonus.

Generally yes. Comparable hotels in Kalimpong usually cost noticeably less than in Darjeeling in peak season, and village homestays around Lava and Lolegaon with meals included often cost ₹1,200–2,200 per person a night, indicative for 2026. Local food and shared transport are similar in price. The savings are biggest outside Puja, Christmas and May holidays.

faqs.q: Is Kalimpong good for families with children and seniors
faqs.a: Yes, with some planning. Kalimpong town has gentle sights, good hotels and short drives. Lava and the villages are higher and colder, with steep steps at some lodges and limited medical help, so pick rooms near the road for seniors. Keep drives under four hours a day, pack warm clothes, and avoid the monsoon months when roads are unreliable.
